senses.gloss:
Dākṣāyaṇa
------------------------------------------
It is a Vedic sacrifice of the kāmya or desire-motivated type. It is a variant of the well-known दर्शपूर्णमास. दक्ष is said to have performed it. Hence the name.
See DARŚAPŪRṆAMĀSA for details.

Dakṣiṇāpatha
------------------------------------------
According to the पुराणस् which contain a lot of geographical and historical material on India, the भारतवर्ष is a part of the जम्बूद्वीप and is divided into seven regions.
Dakṣiṇāpatha is that region which is south of the river नर्मदा. Its extent is about one-fourth of Bāratavarṣa. Some of the people inhabiting this region are: Pāṇḍyas, Keraḷas, Coḷas, Setukas, Mūṣikas, Kumāras, Māhiṣakas, Kāveras, Vidarbhas, Daṇḍakas, Āndhras, Ṛṣikas, Kuntalas and so on.
The modern Deccan region is almost the same as दक्षिणापथ.

Dakṣa
(‘able,’ ‘competent’)
------------------------------------------
A प्रजापति or ड़थेर् of beings, दक्ष is a familiar figure often mentioned in the Hindu mythological literature. There appear to be two Dakṣas, belonging to two different periods known as manvantaras. (See MANVANTARA.)
The first belonged to the Svāyam-bhuva-मन्वन्तर and had married Prasūti, the daughter of the मनु Svayambhū. Out of the 24 daughters he begot in her, सती was one who had been married to शिव.
Once a misunderstanding developed between दक्ष and शिव due to the apparent disrespect shown by the latter. When दक्ष performed a big यज्ञ or sacrifice, he ignored शिव completely and did not invite him. However, सती, due to her filial love towards her ड़थेर् दक्ष, went to attend the same much against her husband शिव’s warning. Being incensed by the callous behaviour of her ड़थेर् she gave up her body in the hall of sacrifice itself in योग. Enraged by this tragedy, शिव got दक्ष’s sacrifice desecrated and destroyed through वीरभद्र, a terrific emanation from himself. दक्ष too was beheaded but was restored to life by the all-merciful शिव at the importunate pleadings of the gods. दक्ष’s regrets and apology once again restored the good relationship between them.
The second दक्ष (of the Cākṣuṣa-मन्वन्तर) was commanded by ब्रह्मा (creator) to proceed with the च्रेअतिओन् of living beings. He did so using his psychic powers. देवस् (Gods), ṛṣis (sages), गन्धर्वस् ( a type of semi-divine beings), असुरस् (demons), sarpas (serpents) apart from human beings were all created by him.
Dakṣa is also the name of an ancient author of a स्मृति (a secondary scripture, a law-book) which is generally called Dakṣasmṛti. The extant work has seven chapters and 220 verses. The topics dealt with are varied. Apart from Varṇāśrama-dharmas, the subjects include the giving of gifts, eulogy of a good housewife, अशौच or ceremonial impurity to be observed on birth or death in one’s family, certain aspects of योग and the philosophy of advaita.

dakṣiṇāgni
(‘the southern fire’)
------------------------------------------
Every āhitāgni—one who ceremonially establishes the Vedic fires—is expected to keep three Vedic fires and the दक्षिणाग्नि is one of them. It is situated within the sacrificial shed, near the main fire (the गार्हपत्य fire), to the south (dakṣiṇa = south). Hence this name. The fire-pit is semicircular or bow-shaped.
This fire is established in various ways among which the following are more common: brought from the गार्हपत्य fire; from the होउसे of a वैश्य or a rich man who has established it by attrition.
It is to be preserved permanently since it protects the sacrificer from evil forces. Some works consider its establishment as optional. It is set up by the ādheya rite which is quite elaborate.
It is also called anvāhāryapacana.
See ANVĀHĀRYA also.

Dakṣiṇāmūrti
(‘form [facing] south’)
------------------------------------------
Though God is one, he assumes three aspects when engaged in the process of सृष्टि (creation), sthiti (preservation) and प्रलय (destruction). They are: ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and शिव (Rudra or महेश्वर).
Out of the several forms of शिव described in the पुराणस् and the आगमस्, the दक्षिणामूर्ति is also one.
It is a benign aspect of his. Since he was facing south (dakṣiṇa = south) at the time of teaching the sages in a secluded spot in the हिमालयस्, he came to be known as दक्षिणामूर्ति. Sometimes the word ‘dakṣiṇā’ is interpreted as ज्ञान, knowledge or wisdom, in which case he represents the very personification of knowledge and wisdom.
He is shown with three eyes, four arms and two legs and is seated under banyan tree. Two of the hands (the front right and the front left) are showing ज्ञानमुद्रा and varadamudrā, postures of imparting knowledge and giving gifts respectively. In the other two hands—the back ones—he is holding the अक्षमाला (rosary) and अग्नि (fire) or a serpent. Sometimes he is pictured as playing on a Vīṇā or lute. Other texts portray him as holding a परशु (axe) and hariṇī (antelope) instead of the rosary and fire. One of the legs is trampling upon the apasmārapuruṣa (cretinous person) signifying इग्नोरन्चे.
The tāntrik works describe him as white in complexion.
He may be shown as surrounded by several ṛṣis or sages eager to learn spiritual wisdom from him.
Several forms of दक्षिणामूर्ति are also described in the tāntrik works. Some of them are: सṁहार-दक्षिणामूर्ति, Lakuṭi-दक्षिणामूर्ति, Medhā-दक्षिणा-mūrti, Sāmba-दक्षिणामूर्ति and so on. Each one of these is, iconographically speaking, sculptured in a different manner.
His worship may involve elaborate rituals. His यन्त्र (magical diagram) is a lotus with eight petals on which the deities ब्रह्मा, सरस्वती, गणपति and some sages are inscribed.
See also ŚIVA.

dakṣiṇā
(‘sacrificial fees’)
------------------------------------------
One of the important items of a Vedic sacrifice is दक्षिणा or the fees to be paid to the priests involved in the conduct of the sacrifice. Generally cows and gold are considered superior among the various kinds of dakṣiṇās. Other animals, articles of ड़ोओद् or anything that will be useful to the donees are also prescribed.
Though it is limited to small quanti-ties in minor rites, fabulous amounts are expected to be given in complicated rites, such as the Rājasūyayāga.
It is interesting to note that a non-ब्राह्मण may be given दक्षिणा if he is learned, whereas, a ब्राह्मण of a different गोत्र (lineage) or who is not learned, is not entitled for it!
A sacrifice where दक्षिणा has not been paid becomes barren and the sacrificer’s life is cut short by this serious defect.
Even the act of giving दक्षिणा is a ritual.

Dakṣiṇācāra
(‘the right [hand] path or conduct’)
------------------------------------------
The religious practices prevalent in the modern Hindu society are influenced greatly by the पुराणस्, the आगमस् and the तन्त्रस्. The तन्त्रस् are mainly works connected with the cult of शक्ति or the Divine मोथेर्.
These tāntrik works present seven types of ācāras or modes of sādhana. They are again regrouped into two: the दक्षिणाचार and the वामाचार.
The worship of the goddess Dakṣiṇa-kālikā, following the Vedic modes of पूजा and sādhanā, as also belief in the varṇāśrama system characterise the दक्षिणाचार.
See also TANTRAS.

Dākṣāyaṇī
(‘Dakṣa’s daughter’)
------------------------------------------
Satī, being the daughter of दक्ष, was also known as दाक्षायणी.
After giving up her body during the sacrifice performed by her ड़थेर् दक्ष, she was reborn as the daughter of Himavān and Menā under the name पार्वती.
See DAKṢA for details.

Dakṣiṇāmūrti Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a short Upaniṣad of 33 verses, assigned to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, but classed among the minor ones. It deals mainly with the meditation on दक्षिणा-mūrti, an aspect of शिव representing a teacher of divine wisdom.
Once, a group of sages under the leadership of शौनक, approached the deathless sage मार्कण्डेय with due respect and asked him how he had attained the cirajīvatva or the deathless state as also eternal bliss. He replied, ‘By the esoteric knowledge of the principle of शिव.’
Then they put him nine questions:
What is that esoteric knowledge of the principle of शिव? Who is the deity in it? Which are the mantras (spiritual formulae)? What is the steadfast devotion needed? What is the means of attaining that knowledge? What is its instrument? What is the offering? What is its final state? What is the final abode?
The esoteric knowledge of शिव is the realisation of him in his aspect as दक्षिणा-mūrti. शिव is called दक्षिणामूर्ति since he can silently give the gift (= दक्षिणा) of Self-knowledge to anyone that is seen by him.
He himself is the deity (= deva) since he shines (deva = one who shines) in his own glory and joy at the time of dissolution of the world.
As regards the mantras, the Upaniṣad offers five of them:
(1) Oṁ namo bhagavate dakṣiṇāmūrtaye
mahyam medhām prajñām
prayaccha स्वाहा ॥
(2) Oṁ dakṣiṇāmūrtir-atarom ॥
(3) Oṁ blūṁ namo hrīm aiṁ
dakṣiṇāmūrtaye jñānaṁ dehi स्वाहा ॥
(4) Oṁ ह्रीṁ śrīṁ sāmbaśivāya
tubhyaṁ svāhā
(5) (Oṁ) namo bhagavate tubhyaṁ vaṭamūlanivāsine ।
vāgīśāya mahājñāna-dāyine māyine namaḥ ॥
The steadfast devotion needed is the conviction that one is ब्रह्मन्, which should last till the death of the body.
The means of attaining that know-ledge is the repetition of the मन्त्र (one of the five already given) with the conscious thinking that one is identical with the deity denoted by the मन्त्र.
The instrument is singular devotion to the मन्त्र.
Offering is the offering of the movement of one’s limbs as worship to the deity of the मन्त्र.
The final state is the attainment of the perfect equanimity of the three guṇas.
And, the final abode is the heart or the सहस्रार (thousand-petalled lotus in the crown of the head) which are the places for the realisation of the Self.
The Upaniṣad ends with the eulogy that one who learns this esoteric wisdom is freed from all sins and attains लिबेरतिओन् from transmigration.
See also DAKṢIṆĀMŪRTI and UPANIṢADS.

Dakṣiṇeśvara
------------------------------------------
Visiting a famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे at least once in a life-time has been a great ambition cherished by all devout Hindus. And, such places of पिल्ग्रिमगे are legion in हिन्दुइस्म्. Many of these pilgrim centres have acquired their importance due to their intimate association with great saints and religious leaders.
दक्षिणेश्वर">Kālī Temple at DakṣiṇeśvaraOne such place, of a rather recent origin, is दक्षिणेश्वर, now a part of the city of Calcutta. Due to its close connection with the life of Śrī रामकृष्ण (A. D. 1836-1886) it is now attracting thousands of votaries and visitors throughout the year.
As one enters the temple complex from the riverside through the landing ghāṭ on the eastern bank of the Ganges river, one comes to the main portico called ‘Cāndni’. On either side of it are the शिव temples six to the north and six to the south. They are all identical. One has to cross the open courtyard to reach the temple of Kālī, the main shrine.
Built by राणी रासमणि (A. D. 1793-1861), a rich landlady, in 1855, this temple of Kālī is the central attraction of this place. The goddess is known as ‘Bhava-tāriṇī’, ‘redeemer from the sufferings of the world’. The image has been carved out of a single piece of basalt and faces south. The deity is standing on the chest of शिव (her spouse) who lies prostrate on a thousand-petalled silver lotus. The height of the image is 85 cms. (33.5 inches) and the shrine-room is 4.5 metres (15 ft.) square excluding the raised plinth and the overall height is more than 33 metres (100 ft.).
Open on all sides and facing the main shrine is the Nāṭmandir (literally, ‘dance-hall’) measuring 22.5 metres (75 ft.) by 15 metres (50 ft.). It is meant for meditation and religio-cultural activities like devotional मुसिच्, dramas and dances with religious themes.
Behind the temple of Kālī stands another temple dedicated to कृष्ण in his Rādhākānta aspect. The images of कृष्ण and राधा are 55 cms. (21.5 inches) and 40 cms. (16 inches) respectively.
Other holy spots in the campus are: Śrī रामकृष्ण’s room, Nahabat and Bakultala ghāṭ, the पञ्चवटी and the Bel tree as also the small cottage or meditation hut.
Śrī रामकृष्ण spent nearly thirty years of his life in that room. The room is about 7 metres (24 ft.) square. The two wooden cots—one smaller than the other—which he was using have been preserved. The room opens on to a semicircular verandah to the west which faces the Ganges river.
The Nahabat or मुसिच् tower is to the north of Śrī रामकृष्ण’s room and has an octagonal room on the ground-floor measuring 2.3 metres (7.75 ft.) across. The entrance door is hardly 1.2 metres (4 ft.) in height. Śrī Sāradā देवी (better known as the Holy मोथेर्) lived in this room. Candrādevī, मोथेर् of Śrī रामकृष्ण, lived on the first floor.
The Bakultala-ghāṭ is the bathing ghāṭ (close to the Nahabat) of the Ganges river, which Śrī Sāradā देवी used to use.
The पञ्चवटी is a grove of five sacred trees intended as a place for spiritual practices. It was renovated by Śrī रामकृष्ण himself.
The Bel tree which is a little away from the पञ्चवटी is the very tree under which Śrī रामकृष्ण practised severe tāntric disciplines guided by भैरवी Brāhmaṇī.
The small cottage is the very meditation room where the great saint attained Advaitic समाधि under the guidance of the monk तोतापुरी.
See also (RĀṆĪ) RĀSAMAṆI and RĀMA-KṚṢṆA.
